4 $(TYPEDEF)
5
6 Supertype for the specialization types. Controls the compilation and
7 function specialization behavior of SciMLFunctions, ultimately controlling
8 the runtime vs compile-time trade-off.

12 """
13 $(TYPEDEF)
14
15 The default specialization level for problem functions. `AutoSpecialize`
16 works by applying a function wrap just-in-time before the solve process
17 to disable just-in-time re-specialization of the solver to the specific
18 choice of model `f` and thus allow for using a cached solver compilation
19 from a different `f`. This wrapping process can lead to a small decreased
20 runtime performance with a benefit of a greatly decreased compile-time.
21
22 ## Note About Benchmarking and Runtime Optimality
23
24 It is recommended that `AutoSpecialize` is not used in any benchmarking
25 due to the potential effect of function wrapping on runtimes. `AutoSpecialize`'s
26 use case is targeted at decreased latency for REPL performance and
27 not for cases where where top runtime performance is required (such as in
28 optimization loops). Generally, for non-stiff equations the cost will be minimal
29 and potentially not even measurable. For stiff equations, function wrapping
30 has the limitation that only chunk sized 1 Dual numbers are allowed, which
31 can decrease Jacobian construction performance.
32
33 ## Limitations of `AutoSpecialize`
34
35 The following limitations are not fundamental to the implementation of `AutoSpecialize`,
36 but are instead chosen as a compromise between default precompilation times and
37 ease of maintenance. Please open an issue to discuss lifting any potential
38 limitations.
39
40 - `AutoSpecialize` is only setup to wrap the functions from in-place ODEs. Other
41 cases are excluded for the time being due to time limitations.
42 - `AutoSpecialize` will only lead to compilation reuse if the ODEFunction's other
43 functions (such as jac and tgrad) are the default `nothing`. These could be
44 JIT wrapped as well in a future version.
45 - `AutoSpecialize`'d functions are only compatible with Jacobian calculations
46 performed with chunk size 1, and only with tag `DiffEqBase.OrdinaryDiffEqTag()`.
47 Thus ODE solvers written on the common interface must be careful to detect
48 the `AutoSpecialize` case and perform differentiation under these constraints,
49 use finite differencing, or manually unwrap before solving. This will lead
50 to decreased runtime performance for sufficiently large Jacobians.
51 - `AutoSpecialize` only wraps on Julia v1.8 and higher.
52 - `AutoSpecialize` does not handle cases with units. If unitful values are detected,
53 wrapping is automatically disabled.
54 - `AutoSpecialize` only wraps cases for which `promote_rule` is defined between `u0`
55 and dual numbers, `u0` and `t`, and for which `ArrayInterface.promote_eltype`
56 is defined on `u0` to dual numbers.
57 - `AutoSpecialize` only wraps cases for which `f.mass_matrix isa UniformScaling`, the
58 default.
59 - `AutoSpecialize` does not wrap cases where `f isa AbstractSciMLOperator`
60 - By default, only the `u0 isa Vector{Float64}`, `eltype(tspan) isa Float64`, and
61 `typeof(p) isa Union{Vector{Float64},SciMLBase.NullParameters}` are specialized
62 by the solver libraries. Other forms can be specialized with
63 `AutoSpecialize`, but must be done in the precompilation of downstream libraries.
64 - `AutoSpecialize`d functions are manually unwrapped in adjoint methods in
65 SciMLSensitivity.jl in order to allow compiler support for automatic differentiation.
66 Improved versions of adjoints which decrease the recompilation surface will come
67 in non-breaking updates.
68
69 Cases where automatic wrapping is disabled are equivalent to `FullSpecialize`.
70
71 ## Example
72
73 ```julia
74 f(du, u, p, t) = (du .= u)
75
76 # Note this is the same as ODEProblem(f, [1.0], (0.0,1.0))
77 # If no preferences are set
78 ODEProblem{true, SciMLBase.AutoSpecialize}(f, [1.0], (0.0, 1.0))
79 ```
80 """
81 struct AutoSpecialize <: AbstractSpecialization end
82
83 """
84 $(TYPEDEF)
85
86 `NoSpecialize` forces SciMLFunctions to not specialize on the types
87 of functions wrapped within it. This ultimately contributes to a
88 form such that every `prob.f` type is the same, meaning compilation
89 caches are fully reused, with the downside of losing runtime performance.
90 `NoSpecialize` is the form that most fully trades off runtime for compile
91 time. Unlike `AutoSpecialize`, `NoSpecialize` can be used with any
92 `SciMLFunction`.
93
94 ## Example
95
96 ```julia
97 f(du, u, p, t) = (du .= u)
98 ODEProblem{true, SciMLBase.NoSpecialize}(f, [1.0], (0.0, 1.0))
99 ```
100 """
101 struct NoSpecialize <: AbstractSpecialization end
102
103 """
104 $(TYPEDEF)
105
106 `FunctionWrapperSpecialize` is an eager wrapping choice which
107 performs a function wrapping during the `ODEProblem` construction.
108 This performs the function wrapping at the earliest possible point,
109 giving the best compile-time vs runtime performance, but with the
110 difficulty that any usage of `prob.f` needs to account for the
111 function wrapper's presence. While optimal in a performance sense,
112 this method has many usability issues with nonstandard solvers
113 and analyses as it requires unwrapping before re-wrapping for any
114 type changes. Thus this method is not used by default. Given that
115 the compile-time different is almost undetectable from AutoSpecialize,
116 this method is mostly used as a benchmarking reference for speed
117 of light for `AutoSpecialize`.
118
119 ## Limitations of `FunctionWrapperSpecialize`
120
121 `FunctionWrapperSpecialize` has all of the limitations of `AutoSpecialize`,
122 but also includes the limitations:
123
124 - `prob.f` is directly specialized to the types of `(u,p,t)`, and any usage
125 of `prob.f` on other types first requires using
126 `SciMLBase.unwrapped_f(prob.f)` to remove the function wrapper.
127 - `FunctionWrapperSpecialize` can only be used by the `ODEProblem` constructor.
128 If an `ODEFunction` is being constructed, the user must manually use
129 `DiffEqBase.wrap_iip` on `f` before calling
130 `ODEFunction{true,FunctionWrapperSpecialize}(f)`. This is a fundamental
131 limitation of the approach as the types of `(u,p,t)` are required in the
132 construction process and not accessible in the `AbstractSciMLFunction` constructors.
133
134 ## Example
135
136 ```julia
137 f(du, u, p, t) = (du .= u)
138 ODEProblem{true, SciMLBase.FunctionWrapperSpecialize}(f, [1.0], (0.0, 1.0))
139 ```
140 """
141 struct FunctionWrapperSpecialize <: AbstractSpecialization end
142
143 """
144 $(TYPEDEF)
145
146 `FullSpecialize` is an eager specialization choice which
147 directly types the `AbstractSciMLFunction` struct to match the type
148 of the model `f`. This forces recompilation of the solver on each
149 new function type `f`, leading to the most compile times with the
150 benefit of having the best runtime performance.
151
152 `FullSpecialize` should be used in all cases where top runtime performance
153 is required, such as in long-running simulations and benchmarking.
154
155 ## Example
156
157 ```julia
158 f(du, u, p, t) = (du .= u)
159 ODEProblem{true, SciMLBase.FullSpecialize}(f, [1.0], (0.0, 1.0))
160 ```
161 """
162 struct FullSpecialize <: AbstractSpecialization end

237 """
238 abstract type AbstractODEFunction{iip} <: AbstractDiffEqFunction{iip} end
239
240 @doc doc"""
241 $(TYPEDEF)
242
243 A representation of an ODE function `f`, defined by:
244
245 ```math
246 M \frac{du}{dt} = f(u,p,t)
247 ```
248
249 and all of its related functions, such as the Jacobian of `f`, its gradient
250 with respect to time, and more. For all cases, `u0` is the initial condition,
251 `p` are the parameters, and `t` is the independent variable.
252
253 ## Constructor
254
255 ```julia
256 ODEFunction{iip,specialize}(f;
257 mass_matrix = __has_mass_matrix(f) ? f.mass_matrix : I,
258 analytic = __has_analytic(f) ? f.analytic : nothing,
259 tgrad= __has_tgrad(f) ? f.tgrad : nothing,
260 jac = __has_jac(f) ? f.jac : nothing,
261 jvp = __has_jvp(f) ? f.jvp : nothing,
262 vjp = __has_vjp(f) ? f.vjp : nothing,
263 jac_prototype = __has_jac_prototype(f) ? f.jac_prototype : nothing,
264 sparsity = __has_sparsity(f) ? f.sparsity : jac_prototype,
265 paramjac = __has_paramjac(f) ? f.paramjac : nothing,
266 colorvec = __has_colorvec(f) ? f.colorvec : nothing,
267 sys = __has_sys(f) ? f.sys : nothing)
268 ```
269
270 Note that only the function `f` itself is required. This function should
271 be given as `f!(du,u,p,t)` or `du = f(u,p,t)`. See the section on `iip`
272 for more details on in-place vs out-of-place handling.
273
274 All of the remaining functions are optional for improving or accelerating
275 the usage of `f`. These include:
276
277 - `mass_matrix`: the mass matrix `M` represented in the ODE function. Can be used
278 to determine that the equation is actually a differential-algebraic equation (DAE)
279 if `M` is singular. Note that in this case special solvers are required, see the
280 DAE solver page for more details: https://docs.sciml.ai/DiffEqDocs/stable/solvers/dae_solve/.
281 Must be an AbstractArray or an AbstractSciMLOperator.
282 - `analytic(u0,p,t)`: used to pass an analytical solution function for the analytical
283 solution of the ODE. Generally only used for testing and development of the solvers.
284 - `tgrad(dT,u,p,t)` or dT=tgrad(u,p,t): returns ``\frac{\partial f(u,p,t)}{\partial t}``
285 - `jac(J,u,p,t)` or `J=jac(u,p,t)`: returns ``\frac{df}{du}``
286 - `jvp(Jv,v,u,p,t)` or `Jv=jvp(v,u,p,t)`: returns the directional derivative``\frac{df}{du} v``
287 - `vjp(Jv,v,u,p,t)` or `Jv=vjp(v,u,p,t)`: returns the adjoint derivative``\frac{df}{du}^\ast v``
288 - `jac_prototype`: a prototype matrix matching the type that matches the Jacobian. For example,
289 if the Jacobian is tridiagonal, then an appropriately sized `Tridiagonal` matrix can be used
290 as the prototype and integrators will specialize on this structure where possible. Non-structured
291 sparsity patterns should use a `SparseMatrixCSC` with a correct sparsity pattern for the Jacobian.
292 The default is `nothing`, which means a dense Jacobian.
293 - `paramjac(pJ,u,p,t)`: returns the parameter Jacobian ``\frac{df}{dp}``.
294 - `colorvec`: a color vector according to the SparseDiffTools.jl definition for the sparsity
295 pattern of the `jac_prototype`. This specializes the Jacobian construction when using
296 finite differences and automatic differentiation to be computed in an accelerated manner
297 based on the sparsity pattern. Defaults to `nothing`, which means a color vector will be
298 internally computed on demand when required. The cost of this operation is highly dependent
299 on the sparsity pattern.
300 ## iip: In-Place vs Out-Of-Place
301
302 `iip` is the optional boolean for determining whether a given function is written to
303 be used in-place or out-of-place. In-place functions are `f!(du,u,p,t)` where the return
304 is ignored, and the result is expected to be mutated into the value of `du`. Out-of-place
305 functions are `du=f(u,p,t)`.
306
307 Normally, this is determined automatically by looking at the method table for `f` and seeing
308 the maximum number of arguments in available dispatches. For this reason, the constructor
309 `ODEFunction(f)` generally works (but is type-unstable). However, for type-stability or
310 to enforce correctness, this option is passed via `ODEFunction{true}(f)`.
311
312 ## specialize: Controlling Compilation and Specialization
313
314 The `specialize` parameter controls the specialization level of the ODEFunction
315 on the function `f`. This allows for a trade-off between compile and run time performance.
316 The available specialization levels are:
317
318 * `SciMLBase.AutoSpecialize`: this form performs a lazy function wrapping on the
319 functions of the ODE in order to stop recompilation of the ODE solver, but allow
320 for the `prob.f` to stay unwrapped for normal usage. This is the default specialization
321 level and strikes a balance in compile time vs runtime performance.
322 * `SciMLBase.FullSpecialize`: this form fully specializes the `ODEFunction` on the
323 constituent functions that make its fields. As such, each `ODEFunction` in this
324 form is uniquely typed, requiring re-specialization and compilation for each new
325 ODE definition. This form has the highest compile-time at the cost of being the
326 most optimal in runtime. This form should be preferred for long-running calculations
327 (such as within optimization loops) and for benchmarking.
328 * `SciMLBase.NoSpecialize`: this form fully unspecializes the function types in the ODEFunction
329 definition by using an `Any` type declaration. As a result, it can result in reduced runtime
330 performance, but is the form that induces the least compile-time.
331 * `SciMLBase.FunctionWrapperSpecialize`: this is an eager function wrapping form. It is
332 unsafe with many solvers, and thus is mostly used for development testing.
333
334 For more details, see the
335 [specialization levels section of the SciMLBase documentation](https://docs.sciml.ai/SciMLBase/stable/interfaces/Problems/#Specialization-Levels).
336
337 ## Fields
338
339 The fields of the ODEFunction type directly match the names of the inputs.
340
341 ## More Details on Jacobians
342
343 The following example creates an inplace `ODEFunction` whose Jacobian is a `Diagonal`:
344
345 ```julia
346 using LinearAlgebra
347 f = (du,u,p,t) -> du .= t .* u
348 jac = (J,u,p,t) -> (J[1,1] = t; J[2,2] = t; J)
349 jp = Diagonal(zeros(2))
350 fun = ODEFunction(f; jac=jac, jac_prototype=jp)
351 ```
352
353 Note that the integrators will always make a deep copy of `fun.jac_prototype`, so
354 there's no worry of aliasing.
355
356 In general, the Jacobian prototype can be anything that has `mul!` defined, in
357 particular sparse matrices or custom lazy types that support `mul!`. A special case
358 is when the `jac_prototype` is a `AbstractSciMLOperator`, in which case you
359 do not need to supply `jac` as it is automatically set to `update_coefficients!`.
360 Refer to the AbstractSciMLOperators documentation for more information
361 on setting up time/parameter dependent operators.
362
363 ## Examples
364
365 ### Declaring Explicit Jacobians for ODEs
366
367 The most standard case, declaring a function for a Jacobian is done by overloading
368 the function `f(du,u,p,t)` with an in-place updating function for the Jacobian:
369 `f_jac(J,u,p,t)` where the value type is used for dispatch. For example,
370 take the Lotka-Volterra model:
371
372 ```julia
373 function f(du,u,p,t)
374 du[1] = 2.0 * u[1] - 1.2 * u[1]*u[2]
375 du[2] = -3 * u[2] + u[1]*u[2]
376 end
377 ```
378
379 To declare the Jacobian, we simply add the dispatch:
380
381 ```julia
382 function f_jac(J,u,p,t)
383 J[1,1] = 2.0 - 1.2 * u[2]
384 J[1,2] = -1.2 * u[1]
385 J[2,1] = 1 * u[2]
386 J[2,2] = -3 + u[1]
387 nothing
388 end
389 ```
390
391 Then we can supply the Jacobian with our ODE as:
392
393 ```julia
394 ff = ODEFunction(f;jac=f_jac)
395 ```
396
397 and use this in an `ODEProblem`:
398
399 ```julia
400 prob = ODEProblem(ff,ones(2),(0.0,10.0))
401 ```
402
403 ## Symbolically Generating the Functions
404
405 See the `modelingtoolkitize` function from
406 [ModelingToolkit.jl](https://docs.sciml.ai/ModelingToolkit/stable/) for
407 automatically symbolically generating the Jacobian and more from the
408 numerically-defined functions.
409 """
410 struct ODEFunction{iip, specialize, F, TMM, Ta, Tt, TJ, JVP, VJP, JP, SP, TW, TWt, WP, TPJ,
411 O, TCV,
412 SYS, ID <: Union{Nothing, OverrideInitData}, NLP <: Union{Nothing, ODENLStepData}} <:
413 AbstractODEFunction{iip}
414 f::F
415 mass_matrix::TMM
416 analytic::Ta
417 tgrad::Tt
418 jac::TJ
419 jvp::JVP
420 vjp::VJP
421 jac_prototype::JP
422 sparsity::SP
423 Wfact::TW
424 Wfact_t::TWt
425 W_prototype::WP
426 paramjac::TPJ
427 observed::O
428 colorvec::TCV
429 sys::SYS
430 initialization_data::ID
431 nlstep_data::NLP
432 end
433
434 @doc doc"""
435 $(TYPEDEF)
436
437 A representation of a split ODE function `f`, defined by:
438
439 ```math
440 M \frac{du}{dt} = f_1(u,p,t) + f_2(u,p,t)
441 ```
442
443 and all of its related functions, such as the Jacobian of `f`, its gradient
444 with respect to time, and more. For all cases, `u0` is the initial condition,
445 `p` are the parameters, and `t` is the independent variable.
446
447 Generally, for ODE integrators the `f_1` portion should be considered the
448 "stiff portion of the model" with larger timescale separation, while the
449 `f_2` portion should be considered the "non-stiff portion". This interpretation
450 is directly used in integrators like IMEX (implicit-explicit integrators)
451 and exponential integrators.
452
453 ## Constructor
454
455 ```julia
456 SplitFunction{iip,specialize}(f1,f2;
457 mass_matrix = __has_mass_matrix(f1) ? f1.mass_matrix : I,
458 analytic = __has_analytic(f1) ? f1.analytic : nothing,
459 tgrad= __has_tgrad(f1) ? f1.tgrad : nothing,
460 jac = __has_jac(f1) ? f1.jac : nothing,
461 jvp = __has_jvp(f1) ? f1.jvp : nothing,
462 vjp = __has_vjp(f1) ? f1.vjp : nothing,
463 jac_prototype = __has_jac_prototype(f1) ? f1.jac_prototype : nothing,
464 W_prototype = __has_W_prototype(f1) ? f1.W_prototype : nothing,
465 sparsity = __has_sparsity(f1) ? f1.sparsity : jac_prototype,
466 paramjac = __has_paramjac(f1) ? f1.paramjac : nothing,
467 colorvec = __has_colorvec(f1) ? f1.colorvec : nothing,
468 sys = __has_sys(f1) ? f1.sys : nothing)
469 ```
470
471 Note that only the functions `f_i` themselves are required. These functions should
472 be given as `f_i!(du,u,p,t)` or `du = f_i(u,p,t)`. See the section on `iip`
473 for more details on in-place vs out-of-place handling.
474
475 All of the remaining functions are optional for improving or accelerating
476 the usage of the `SplitFunction`. These include:
477
478 - `mass_matrix`: the mass matrix `M` represented in the ODE function. Can be used
479 to determine that the equation is actually a differential-algebraic equation (DAE)
480 if `M` is singular. Note that in this case special solvers are required, see the
481 DAE solver page for more details: https://docs.sciml.ai/DiffEqDocs/stable/solvers/dae_solve/.
482 Must be an AbstractArray or an AbstractSciMLOperator.
483 - `analytic(u0,p,t)`: used to pass an analytical solution function for the analytical
484 solution of the ODE. Generally only used for testing and development of the solvers.
485 - `tgrad(dT,u,p,t)` or dT=tgrad(u,p,t): returns ``\frac{\partial f_1(u,p,t)}{\partial t}``
486 - `jac(J,u,p,t)` or `J=jac(u,p,t)`: returns ``\frac{df_1}{du}``
487 - `jvp(Jv,v,u,p,t)` or `Jv=jvp(v,u,p,t)`: returns the directional derivative ``\frac{df_1}{du} v``
488 - `vjp(Jv,v,u,p,t)` or `Jv=vjp(v,u,p,t)`: returns the adjoint derivative ``\frac{df_1}{du}^\ast v``
489 - `jac_prototype`: a prototype matrix matching the type that matches the Jacobian. For example,
490 if the Jacobian is tridiagonal, then an appropriately sized `Tridiagonal` matrix can be used
491 as the prototype and integrators will specialize on this structure where possible. Non-structured
492 sparsity patterns should use a `SparseMatrixCSC` with a correct sparsity pattern for the Jacobian.
493 The default is `nothing`, which means a dense Jacobian.
494 - `W_prototype`: a prototype matrix matching the type that matches the W matrix. For example,
495 if the Jacobian is tridiagonal, and the mass_matrix is diagonal, then an appropriately sized `Tridiagonal`
496 matrix can be used as the prototype and integrators will specialize on this structure where possible. Non-structured
497 sparsity patterns should use a `SparseMatrixCSC` with a correct sparsity pattern for the W matrix.
498 The default is `nothing`, which means a W of appropriate type for the jacobian and linear solver
499 - `paramjac(pJ,u,p,t)`: returns the parameter Jacobian ``\frac{df_1}{dp}``.
500 - `colorvec`: a color vector according to the SparseDiffTools.jl definition for the sparsity
501 pattern of the `jac_prototype`. This specializes the Jacobian construction when using
502 finite differences and automatic differentiation to be computed in an accelerated manner
503 based on the sparsity pattern. Defaults to `nothing`, which means a color vector will be
504 internally computed on demand when required. The cost of this operation is highly dependent
505 on the sparsity pattern.
506
507 ## Note on the Derivative Definition
508
509 The derivatives, such as the Jacobian, are only defined on the `f1` portion of the split ODE.
510 This is used to treat the `f1` implicit while keeping the `f2` portion explicit.
511
512 ## iip: In-Place vs Out-Of-Place
513
514 For more details on this argument, see the ODEFunction documentation.
515
516 ## specialize: Controlling Compilation and Specialization
517
518 For more details on this argument, see the ODEFunction documentation.
519
520 ## Fields
521
522 The fields of the SplitFunction type directly match the names of the inputs.
523
524 ## Symbolically Generating the Functions
525
526 See the `modelingtoolkitize` function from
527 [ModelingToolkit.jl](https://docs.sciml.ai/ModelingToolkit/stable/) for
528 automatically symbolically generating the Jacobian and more from the
529 numerically-defined functions. See `ModelingToolkit.SplitODEProblem` for
530 information on generating the SplitFunction from this symbolic engine.
531 """
532 struct SplitFunction{
533 iip, specialize, F1, F2, TMM, C, Ta, Tt, TJ, JVP, VJP, JP, WP, SP, TW, TWt,
534 TPJ, O, TCV, SYS, ID <: Union{Nothing, OverrideInitData},
535 NLP <: Union{Nothing, ODENLStepData}} <: AbstractODEFunction{iip}
536 f1::F1
537 f2::F2
538 mass_matrix::TMM
539 _func_cache::C
540 analytic::Ta
541 tgrad::Tt
542 jac::TJ
543 jvp::JVP
544 vjp::VJP
545 jac_prototype::JP
546 W_prototype::WP
547 sparsity::SP
548 Wfact::TW
549 Wfact_t::TWt
550 paramjac::TPJ
551 observed::O
552 colorvec::TCV
553 sys::SYS
554 initialization_data::ID
555 nlstep_data::NLP
556 end

558 @doc doc"""
559 $(TYPEDEF)
560
561 A representation of an ODE function `f`, defined by:
562
563 ```math
564 M \frac{du}{dt} = f(u,p,t)
565 ```
566
567 as a partitioned ODE:
568
569 ```math
570 \begin{align}
571 M_1 \frac{du}{dt} = f_1(u,p,t) \\
572 M_2 \frac{du}{dt} = f_2(u,p,t)
573 \end{align}
574 ```
575
576 and all of its related functions, such as the Jacobian of `f`, its gradient
577 with respect to time, and more. For all cases, `u0` is the initial condition,
578 `p` are the parameters, and `t` is the independent variable.
579
580 ## Constructor
581
582 ```julia
583 DynamicalODEFunction{iip,specialize}(f1,f2;
584 mass_matrix = __has_mass_matrix(f) ? f.mass_matrix : I,
585 analytic = __has_analytic(f) ? f.analytic : nothing,
586 tgrad= __has_tgrad(f) ? f.tgrad : nothing,
587 jac = __has_jac(f) ? f.jac : nothing,
588 jvp = __has_jvp(f) ? f.jvp : nothing,
589 vjp = __has_vjp(f) ? f.vjp : nothing,
590 jac_prototype = __has_jac_prototype(f) ? f.jac_prototype : nothing,
591 sparsity = __has_sparsity(f) ? f.sparsity : jac_prototype,
592 paramjac = __has_paramjac(f) ? f.paramjac : nothing,
593 colorvec = __has_colorvec(f) ? f.colorvec : nothing,
594 sys = __has_sys(f) ? f.sys : nothing)
595 ```
596
597 Note that only the functions `f_i` themselves are required. These functions should
598 be given as `f_i!(du,u,p,t)` or `du = f_i(u,p,t)`. See the section on `iip`
599 for more details on in-place vs out-of-place handling.
600
601 All of the remaining functions are optional for improving or accelerating
602 the usage of `f`. These include:
603
604 - `mass_matrix`: the mass matrix `M_i` represented in the ODE function. Can be used
605 to determine that the equation is actually a differential-algebraic equation (DAE)
606 if `M` is singular. Note that in this case special solvers are required, see the
607 DAE solver page for more details: <https://docs.sciml.ai/DiffEqDocs/stable/solvers/dae_solve/>.
608 Must be an AbstractArray or an AbstractSciMLOperator. Should be given as a tuple
609 of mass matrices, i.e. `(M_1, M_2)` for the mass matrices of equations 1 and 2
610 respectively.
611 - `analytic(u0,p,t)`: used to pass an analytical solution function for the analytical
612 solution of the ODE. Generally only used for testing and development of the solvers.
613 - `tgrad(dT,u,p,t)` or dT=tgrad(u,p,t): returns ``\frac{\partial f(u,p,t)}{\partial t}``
614 - `jac(J,u,p,t)` or `J=jac(u,p,t)`: returns ``\frac{df}{du}``
615 - `jvp(Jv,v,u,p,t)` or `Jv=jvp(v,u,p,t)`: returns the directional derivative ``\frac{df}{du} v``
616 - `vjp(Jv,v,u,p,t)` or `Jv=vjp(v,u,p,t)`: returns the adjoint derivative ``\frac{df}{du}^\ast v``
617 - `jac_prototype`: a prototype matrix matching the type that matches the Jacobian. For example,
618 if the Jacobian is tridiagonal, then an appropriately sized `Tridiagonal` matrix can be used
619 as the prototype and integrators will specialize on this structure where possible. Non-structured
620 sparsity patterns should use a `SparseMatrixCSC` with a correct sparsity pattern for the Jacobian.
621 The default is `nothing`, which means a dense Jacobian.
622 - `paramjac(pJ,u,p,t)`: returns the parameter Jacobian ``\frac{df}{dp}``.
623 - `colorvec`: a color vector according to the SparseDiffTools.jl definition for the sparsity
624 pattern of the `jac_prototype`. This specializes the Jacobian construction when using
625 finite differences and automatic differentiation to be computed in an accelerated manner
626 based on the sparsity pattern. Defaults to `nothing`, which means a color vector will be
627 internally computed on demand when required. The cost of this operation is highly dependent
628 on the sparsity pattern.
629
630 ## iip: In-Place vs Out-Of-Place
631
632 For more details on this argument, see the ODEFunction documentation.
633
634 ## specialize: Controlling Compilation and Specialization
635
636 For more details on this argument, see the ODEFunction documentation.
637
638 ## Fields
639
640 The fields of the DynamicalODEFunction type directly match the names of the inputs.
641 """
642 struct DynamicalODEFunction{iip, specialize, F1, F2, TMM, Ta, Tt, TJ, JVP, VJP, JP, SP, TW,
643 TWt, TPJ,
644 O, TCV, SYS, ID} <: AbstractODEFunction{iip}
645 f1::F1
646 f2::F2
647 mass_matrix::TMM
648 analytic::Ta
649 tgrad::Tt
650 jac::TJ
651 jvp::JVP
652 vjp::VJP
653 jac_prototype::JP
654 sparsity::SP
655 Wfact::TW
656 Wfact_t::TWt
657 paramjac::TPJ
658 observed::O
659 colorvec::TCV
660 sys::SYS
661 initialization_data::ID
662 end

1013 jvp = __has_jvp(f) ? f.jvp : nothing,
1014 vjp = __has_vjp(f) ? f.vjp : nothing,
1015 ggprime = nothing,
1016 jac_prototype = __has_jac_prototype(f) ? f.jac_prototype : nothing,

1018 paramjac = __has_paramjac(f) ? f.paramjac : nothing,
1019 colorvec = __has_colorvec(f) ? f.colorvec : nothing,
1020 sys = __has_sys(f) ? f.sys : nothing)
1021 ```

1024 be given as `f!(du,u,p,t)` or `du = f(u,p,t)`. See the section on `iip`
1025 for more details on in-place vs out-of-place handling.
1026
1027 All of the remaining functions are optional for improving or accelerating
1028 the usage of `f`. These include:
1029
1030 - `mass_matrix`: the mass matrix `M` represented in the ODE function. Can be used
1031 to determine that the equation is actually a differential-algebraic equation (DAE)
1032 if `M` is singular. Note that in this case special solvers are required, see the
1033 DAE solver page for more details: https://docs.sciml.ai/DiffEqDocs/stable/solvers/dae_solve/.
1034 Must be an AbstractArray or an AbstractSciMLOperator.
1035 - `analytic(u0,p,t)`: used to pass an analytical solution function for the analytical
1036 solution of the ODE. Generally only used for testing and development of the solvers.
1037 - `tgrad(dT,u,p,t)` or dT=tgrad(u,p,t): returns ``\frac{\partial f(u,p,t)}{\partial t}``
1038 - `jac(J,u,p,t)` or `J=jac(u,p,t)`: returns ``\frac{df}{du}``
1039 - `jvp(Jv,v,u,p,t)` or `Jv=jvp(v,u,p,t)`: returns the directional derivative ``\frac{df}{du} v``
1040 - `vjp(Jv,v,u,p,t)` or `Jv=vjp(v,u,p,t)`: returns the adjoint derivative ``\frac{df}{du}^\ast v``
1041 - `ggprime(J,u,p,t)` or `J = ggprime(u,p,t)`: returns the Milstein derivative
1042 ``\frac{dg(u,p,t)}{du} g(u,p,t)``
1043 - `jac_prototype`: a prototype matrix matching the type that matches the Jacobian. For example,
1044 if the Jacobian is tridiagonal, then an appropriately sized `Tridiagonal` matrix can be used
1045 as the prototype and integrators will specialize on this structure where possible. Non-structured
1046 sparsity patterns should use a `SparseMatrixCSC` with a correct sparsity pattern for the Jacobian.
1047 The default is `nothing`, which means a dense Jacobian.
1048 - `paramjac(pJ,u,p,t)`: returns the parameter Jacobian ``\frac{df}{dp}``.
1049 - `colorvec`: a color vector according to the SparseDiffTools.jl definition for the sparsity
1050 pattern of the `jac_prototype`. This specializes the Jacobian construction when using
1051 finite differences and automatic differentiation to be computed in an accelerated manner
1052 based on the sparsity pattern. Defaults to `nothing`, which means a color vector will be
1053 internally computed on demand when required. The cost of this operation is highly dependent
1054 on the sparsity pattern.
1055

1057
1058 For more details on this argument, see the ODEFunction documentation.
1059

1061

1063
1064 ## Fields
1065
1066 The fields of the ODEFunction type directly match the names of the inputs.
1067 """
1068 struct SDEFunction{iip, specialize, F, G, TMM, Ta, Tt, TJ, JVP, VJP, JP, SP, TW, TWt, TPJ,
1069 GG, O,
1070 TCV, SYS, ID

1092 @doc doc"""
1093 $(TYPEDEF)
1094
1095 A representation of a split SDE function `f`, defined by:
1096
1097 ```math
1098 M \frac{du}{dt} = f_1(u,p,t) + f_2(u,p,t) + g(u,p,t) dW
1099 ```
1100
1101 and all of its related functions, such as the Jacobian of `f`, its gradient
1102 with respect to time, and more. For all cases, `u0` is the initial condition,
1103 `p` are the parameters, and `t` is the independent variable.
1104
1105 Generally, for SDE integrators the `f_1` portion should be considered the
1106 "stiff portion of the model" with larger timescale separation, while the
1107 `f_2` portion should be considered the "non-stiff portion". This interpretation
1108 is directly used in integrators like IMEX (implicit-explicit integrators)
1109 and exponential integrators.
1110
1111 ## Constructor
1112
1113 ```julia
1114 SplitSDEFunction{iip,specialize}(f1,f2,g;
1115 mass_matrix = __has_mass_matrix(f) ? f.mass_matrix : I,
1116 analytic = __has_analytic(f) ? f.analytic : nothing,
1117 tgrad= __has_tgrad(f) ? f.tgrad : nothing,
1118 jac = __has_jac(f) ? f.jac : nothing,
1119 jvp = __has_jvp(f) ? f.jvp : nothing,
1120 vjp = __has_vjp(f) ? f.vjp : nothing,
1121 ggprime = nothing,
1122 jac_prototype = __has_jac_prototype(f) ? f.jac_prototype : nothing,
1123 sparsity = __has_sparsity(f) ? f.sparsity : jac_prototype,
1124 paramjac = __has_paramjac(f) ? f.paramjac : nothing,
1125 colorvec = __has_colorvec(f) ? f.colorvec : nothing,
1126 sys = __has_sys(f) ? f.sys : nothing)
1127 ```
1128
1129 Note that only the function `f` itself is required. All of the remaining functions
1130 are optional for improving or accelerating the usage of `f`. These include:
1131
1132 - `mass_matrix`: the mass matrix `M` represented in the SDE function. Can be used
1133 to determine that the equation is actually a stochastic differential-algebraic equation (SDAE)
1134 if `M` is singular. Note that in this case special solvers are required, see the
1135 DAE solver page for more details: https://docs.sciml.ai/DiffEqDocs/stable/solvers/sdae_solve/.
1136 Must be an AbstractArray or an AbstractSciMLOperator.
1137 - `analytic(u0,p,t)`: used to pass an analytical solution function for the analytical
1138 solution of the ODE. Generally only used for testing and development of the solvers.
1139 - `tgrad(dT,u,p,t)` or dT=tgrad(u,p,t): returns ``\frac{\partial f_1(u,p,t)}{\partial t}``
1140 - `jac(J,u,p,t)` or `J=jac(u,p,t)`: returns ``\frac{df_1}{du}``
1141 - `jvp(Jv,v,u,p,t)` or `Jv=jvp(v,u,p,t)`: returns the directional derivative``\frac{df_1}{du} v``
1142 - `vjp(Jv,v,u,p,t)` or `Jv=vjp(v,u,p,t)`: returns the adjoint derivative``\frac{df_1}{du}^\ast v``
1143 - `ggprime(J,u,p,t)` or `J = ggprime(u,p,t)`: returns the Milstein derivative
1144 ``\frac{dg(u,p,t)}{du} g(u,p,t)``
1145 - `jac_prototype`: a prototype matrix matching the type that matches the Jacobian. For example,
1146 if the Jacobian is tridiagonal, then an appropriately sized `Tridiagonal` matrix can be used
1147 as the prototype and integrators will specialize on this structure where possible. Non-structured
1148 sparsity patterns should use a `SparseMatrixCSC` with a correct sparsity pattern for the Jacobian.
1149 The default is `nothing`, which means a dense Jacobian.
1150 - `paramjac(pJ,u,p,t)`: returns the parameter Jacobian ``\frac{df_1}{dp}``.
1151 - `colorvec`: a color vector according to the SparseDiffTools.jl definition for the sparsity
1152 pattern of the `jac_prototype`. This specializes the Jacobian construction when using
1153 finite differences and automatic differentiation to be computed in an accelerated manner
1154 based on the sparsity pattern. Defaults to `nothing`, which means a color vector will be
1155 internally computed on demand when required. The cost of this operation is highly dependent
1156 on the sparsity pattern.
1157
1158 ## Note on the Derivative Definition
1159
1160 The derivatives, such as the Jacobian, are only defined on the `f1` portion of the split ODE.
1161 This is used to treat the `f1` implicit while keeping the `f2` portion explicit.
1162
1163 ## iip: In-Place vs Out-Of-Place
1164
1165 For more details on this argument, see the ODEFunction documentation.
1166
1167 ## specialize: Controlling Compilation and Specialization
1168
1169 For more details on this argument, see the ODEFunction documentation.
1170
1171 ## Fields
1172
1173 The fields of the SplitSDEFunction type directly match the names of the inputs.
1174 """
1175 struct SplitSDEFunction{iip, specialize, F1, F2, G, TMM, C, Ta, Tt, TJ, JVP, VJP, JP, SP,
1176 TW,
1177 TWt, TPJ,
1178 O, TCV, SYS, ID} <: AbstractSDEFunction{iip}
1179 f1::F1
1180 f2::F2
1181 g::G
1182 mass_matrix::TMM
1183 _func_cache::C
1184 analytic::Ta
1185 tgrad::Tt
1186 jac::TJ
1187 jvp::JVP
1188 vjp::VJP
1189 jac_prototype::JP
1190 sparsity::SP
1191 Wfact::TW
1192 Wfact_t::TWt
1193 paramjac::TPJ
1194 observed::O
1195 colorvec::TCV
1196 sys::SYS
1197 initialization_data::ID
1198 end

1200 @doc doc"""
1201 $(TYPEDEF)
1202
1203 A representation of an SDE function `f` and `g`, defined by:
1204
1205 ```math
1206 M du = f(u,p,t) dt + g(u,p,t) dW_t
1207 ```
1208
1209 as a partitioned ODE:
1210
1211 ```math
1212 \begin{align}
1213 M_1 du = f_1(u,p,t) dt + g(u,p,t) dW_t \\
1214 M_2 du = f_2(u,p,t) dt + g(u,p,t) dW_t
1215 \end{align}
1216 ```
1217
1218 and all of its related functions, such as the Jacobian of `f`, its gradient
1219 with respect to time, and more. For all cases, `u0` is the initial condition,
1220 `p` are the parameters, and `t` is the independent variable.
1221
1222 ## Constructor
1223
1224 ```julia
1225 DynamicalSDEFunction{iip,specialize}(f1,f2;
1226 mass_matrix = __has_mass_matrix(f) ? f.mass_matrix : I,
1227 analytic = __has_analytic(f) ? f.analytic : nothing,
1228 tgrad= __has_tgrad(f) ? f.tgrad : nothing,
1229 jac = __has_jac(f) ? f.jac : nothing,
1230 jvp = __has_jvp(f) ? f.jvp : nothing,
1231 vjp = __has_vjp(f) ? f.vjp : nothing,
1232 ggprime=nothing,
1233 jac_prototype = __has_jac_prototype(f) ? f.jac_prototype : nothing,
1234 sparsity = __has_sparsity(f) ? f.sparsity : jac_prototype,
1235 paramjac = __has_paramjac(f) ? f.paramjac : nothing,
1236 colorvec = __has_colorvec(f) ? f.colorvec : nothing,
1237 sys = __has_sys(f) ? f.sys : nothing)
1238 ```
1239
1240 Note that only the functions `f_i` themselves are required. These functions should
1241 be given as `f_i!(du,u,p,t)` or `du = f_i(u,p,t)`. See the section on `iip`
1242 for more details on in-place vs out-of-place handling.
1243
1244 All of the remaining functions are optional for improving or accelerating
1245 the usage of `f`. These include:
1246
1247 - `mass_matrix`: the mass matrix `M_i` represented in the ODE function. Can be used
1248 to determine that the equation is actually a differential-algebraic equation (DAE)
1249 if `M` is singular. Note that in this case special solvers are required, see the
1250 DAE solver page for more details: https://docs.sciml.ai/DiffEqDocs/stable/dae_solve/.
1251 Must be an AbstractArray or an AbstractSciMLOperator. Should be given as a tuple
1252 of mass matrices, i.e. `(M_1, M_2)` for the mass matrices of equations 1 and 2
1253 respectively.
1254 - `analytic(u0,p,t)`: used to pass an analytical solution function for the analytical
1255 solution of the ODE. Generally only used for testing and development of the solvers.
1256 - `tgrad(dT,u,p,t)` or dT=tgrad(u,p,t): returns ``\frac{\partial f(u,p,t)}{\partial t}``
1257 - `jac(J,u,p,t)` or `J=jac(u,p,t)`: returns ``\frac{df}{du}``
1258 - `jvp(Jv,v,u,p,t)` or `Jv=jvp(v,u,p,t)`: returns the directional derivative``\frac{df}{du} v``
1259 - `vjp(Jv,v,u,p,t)` or `Jv=vjp(v,u,p,t)`: returns the adjoint derivative``\frac{df}{du}^\ast v``
1260 - `ggprime(J,u,p,t)` or `J = ggprime(u,p,t)`: returns the Milstein derivative
1261 ``\frac{dg(u,p,t)}{du} g(u,p,t)``
1262 - `jac_prototype`: a prototype matrix matching the type that matches the Jacobian. For example,
1263 if the Jacobian is tridiagonal, then an appropriately sized `Tridiagonal` matrix can be used
1264 as the prototype and integrators will specialize on this structure where possible. Non-structured
1265 sparsity patterns should use a `SparseMatrixCSC` with a correct sparsity pattern for the Jacobian.
1266 The default is `nothing`, which means a dense Jacobian.
1267 - `paramjac(pJ,u,p,t)`: returns the parameter Jacobian ``\frac{df}{dp}``.
1268 - `colorvec`: a color vector according to the SparseDiffTools.jl definition for the sparsity
1269 pattern of the `jac_prototype`. This specializes the Jacobian construction when using
1270 finite differences and automatic differentiation to be computed in an accelerated manner
1271 based on the sparsity pattern. Defaults to `nothing`, which means a color vector will be
1272 internally computed on demand when required. The cost of this operation is highly dependent
1273 on the sparsity pattern.
1274
1275 ## iip: In-Place vs Out-Of-Place
1276
1277 For more details on this argument, see the ODEFunction documentation.
1278
1279 ## specialize: Controlling Compilation and Specialization
1280
1281 For more details on this argument, see the ODEFunction documentation.
1282
1283 ## Fields
1284
1285 The fields of the DynamicalSDEFunction type directly match the names of the inputs.
1286 """
1287 struct DynamicalSDEFunction{iip, specialize, F1, F2, G, TMM, C, Ta, Tt, TJ, JVP, VJP, JP,
1288 SP,
1289 TW, TWt,
1290 TPJ, O, TCV, SYS, ID} <: AbstractSDEFunction{iip}
1291 # This is a direct copy of the SplitSDEFunction, maybe it's not necessary and the above can be used instead.
1292 f1::F1

1295 mass_matrix::TMM

1298 tgrad::Tt
1299 jac::TJ
1300 jvp::JVP
1301 vjp::VJP
1302 jac_prototype::JP
1303 sparsity::SP
1304 Wfact::TW
1305 Wfact_t::TWt

1315 """
1316 abstract type AbstractRODEFunction{iip} <: AbstractDiffEqFunction{iip} end
1317
1318 @doc doc"""
1319 $(TYPEDEF)
1320
1321 A representation of a RODE function `f`, defined by:
1322
1323 ```math
1324 M \frac{du}{dt} = f(u,p,t,W)dt
1325 ```
1326
1327 and all of its related functions, such as the Jacobian of `f`, its gradient
1328 with respect to time, and more. For all cases, `u0` is the initial condition,
1329 `p` are the parameters, and `t` is the independent variable.
1330
1331 ## Constructor
1332
1333 ```julia
1334 RODEFunction{iip,specialize}(f;
1335 mass_matrix = __has_mass_matrix(f) ? f.mass_matrix : I,
1336 analytic = __has_analytic(f) ? f.analytic : nothing,
1337 tgrad= __has_tgrad(f) ? f.tgrad : nothing,
1338 jac = __has_jac(f) ? f.jac : nothing,
1339 jvp = __has_jvp(f) ? f.jvp : nothing,
1340 vjp = __has_vjp(f) ? f.vjp : nothing,
1341 jac_prototype = __has_jac_prototype(f) ? f.jac_prototype : nothing,
1342 sparsity = __has_sparsity(f) ? f.sparsity : jac_prototype,
1343 paramjac = __has_paramjac(f) ? f.paramjac : nothing,
1344 colorvec = __has_colorvec(f) ? f.colorvec : nothing,
1345 sys = __has_sys(f) ? f.sys : nothing,
1346 analytic_full = __has_analytic_full(f) ? f.analytic_full : false)
1347 ```
1348
1349 Note that only the function `f` itself is required. This function should
1350 be given as `f!(du,u,p,t,W)` or `du = f(u,p,t,W)`. See the section on `iip`
1351 for more details on in-place vs out-of-place handling.
1352
1353 All of the remaining functions are optional for improving or accelerating
1354 the usage of `f`. These include:
1355
1356 - `mass_matrix`: the mass matrix `M` represented in the RODE function. Can be used
1357 to determine that the equation is actually a random differential-algebraic equation (RDAE)
1358 if `M` is singular.
1359 - `analytic`: (u0,p,t,W)` or `analytic(sol)`: used to pass an analytical solution function for the analytical
1360 solution of the RODE. Generally only used for testing and development of the solvers.
1361 The exact form depends on the field `analytic_full`.
1362 - `analytic_full`: a boolean to indicate whether to use the form `analytic(u0,p,t,W)` (if `false`)
1363 or the form `analytic!(sol)` (if `true`). The former is expected to return the solution `u(t)` of
1364 the equation, given the initial condition `u0`, the parameter `p`, the current time `t` and the
1365 value `W=W(t)` of the noise at the given time `t`. The latter case is useful when the solution
1366 of the RODE depends on the whole history of the noise, which is available in `sol.W.W`, at
1367 times `sol.W.t`. In this case, `analytic(sol)` must mutate explicitly the field `sol.u_analytic`
1368 with the corresponding expected solution at `sol.W.t` or `sol.t`.
1369 - `tgrad(dT,u,p,t,W)` or dT=tgrad(u,p,t,W): returns ``\frac{\partial f(u,p,t,W)}{\partial t}``
1370 - `jac(J,u,p,t,W)` or `J=jac(u,p,t,W)`: returns ``\frac{df}{du}``
1371 - `jvp(Jv,v,u,p,t,W)` or `Jv=jvp(v,u,p,t,W)`: returns the directional derivative ``\frac{df}{du} v``
1372 - `vjp(Jv,v,u,p,t,W)` or `Jv=vjp(v,u,p,t,W)`: returns the adjoint derivative ``\frac{df}{du}^\ast v``
1373 - `jac_prototype`: a prototype matrix matching the type that matches the Jacobian. For example,
1374 if the Jacobian is tridiagonal, then an appropriately sized `Tridiagonal` matrix can be used
1375 as the prototype and integrators will specialize on this structure where possible. Non-structured
1376 sparsity patterns should use a `SparseMatrixCSC` with a correct sparsity pattern for the Jacobian.
1377 The default is `nothing`, which means a dense Jacobian.
1378 - `paramjac(pJ,u,p,t,W)`: returns the parameter Jacobian ``\frac{df}{dp}``.
1379 - `colorvec`: a color vector according to the SparseDiffTools.jl definition for the sparsity
1380 pattern of the `jac_prototype`. This specializes the Jacobian construction when using
1381 finite differences and automatic differentiation to be computed in an accelerated manner
1382 based on the sparsity pattern. Defaults to `nothing`, which means a color vector will be
1383 internally computed on demand when required. The cost of this operation is highly dependent
1384 on the sparsity pattern.
1385
1386 ## iip: In-Place vs Out-Of-Place
1387
1388 For more details on this argument, see the ODEFunction documentation.
1389
1390 ## specialize: Controlling Compilation and Specialization
1391
1392 For more details on this argument, see the ODEFunction documentation.
1393
1394 ## Fields
1395
1396 The fields of the RODEFunction type directly match the names of the inputs.
1397 """
1398 struct RODEFunction{
1399 iip, specialize, F, TMM, Ta, Tt, TJ, JVP, VJP, JP, SP, TW, TWt, TPJ, O, TCV, SYS,
1400 ID
1401 } <:
1402 AbstractRODEFunction{iip}
1403 f::F
1404 mass_matrix::TMM
1405 analytic::Ta
1406 tgrad::Tt
1407 jac::TJ
1408 jvp::JVP
1409 vjp::VJP
1410 jac_prototype::JP
1411 sparsity::SP
1412 Wfact::TW
1413 Wfact_t::TWt
1414 paramjac::TPJ
1415 observed::O
1416 colorvec::TCV
1417 sys::SYS
1418 analytic_full::Bool
1419 initialization_data::ID
1420 end
1421
1422 """

1424 """
1425 abstract type AbstractDAEFunction{iip} <: AbstractDiffEqFunction{iip} end
1426
1427 @doc doc"""
1428 $(TYPEDEF)
1429
1430 A representation of an implicit DAE function `f`, defined by:
1431
1432 ```math
1433 0 = f(\frac{du}{dt},u,p,t)
1434 ```
1435
1436 and all of its related functions, such as the Jacobian of `f`, its gradient
1437 with respect to time, and more. For all cases, `u0` is the initial condition,
1438 `p` are the parameters, and `t` is the independent variable.
1439
1440 ## Constructor
1441
1442 ```julia
1443 DAEFunction{iip,specialize}(f;
1444 analytic = __has_analytic(f) ? f.analytic : nothing,
1445 jac = __has_jac(f) ? f.jac : nothing,
1446 jvp = __has_jvp(f) ? f.jvp : nothing,
1447 vjp = __has_vjp(f) ? f.vjp : nothing,
1448 jac_prototype = __has_jac_prototype(f) ? f.jac_prototype : nothing,
1449 sparsity = __has_sparsity(f) ? f.sparsity : jac_prototype,
1450 colorvec = __has_colorvec(f) ? f.colorvec : nothing,
1451 sys = __has_sys(f) ? f.sys : nothing)
1452 ```
1453
1454 Note that only the function `f` itself is required. This function should
1455 be given as `f!(out,du,u,p,t)` or `out = f(du,u,p,t)`. See the section on `iip`
1456 for more details on in-place vs out-of-place handling.
1457
1458 All of the remaining functions are optional for improving or accelerating
1459 the usage of `f`. These include:
1460
1461 - `analytic(u0,p,t)`: used to pass an analytical solution function for the analytical
1462 solution of the ODE. Generally only used for testing and development of the solvers.
1463 - `jac(J,du,u,p,gamma,t)` or `J=jac(du,u,p,gamma,t)`: returns the implicit DAE Jacobian
1464 defined as ``gamma \frac{dG}{d(du)} + \frac{dG}{du}``
1465 - `jvp(Jv,v,du,u,p,gamma,t)` or `Jv=jvp(v,du,u,p,gamma,t)`: returns the directional
1466 derivative``\frac{df}{du} v``
1467 - `vjp(Jv,v,du,u,p,gamma,t)` or `Jv=vjp(v,du,u,p,gamma,t)`: returns the adjoint
1468 derivative``\frac{df}{du}^\ast v``
1469 - `jac_prototype`: a prototype matrix matching the type that matches the Jacobian. For example,
1470 if the Jacobian is tridiagonal, then an appropriately sized `Tridiagonal` matrix can be used
1471 as the prototype and integrators will specialize on this structure where possible. Non-structured
1472 sparsity patterns should use a `SparseMatrixCSC` with a correct sparsity pattern for the Jacobian.
1473 The default is `nothing`, which means a dense Jacobian.
1474 - `colorvec`: a color vector according to the SparseDiffTools.jl definition for the sparsity
1475 pattern of the `jac_prototype`. This specializes the Jacobian construction when using
1476 finite differences and automatic differentiation to be computed in an accelerated manner
1477 based on the sparsity pattern. Defaults to `nothing`, which means a color vector will be
1478 internally computed on demand when required. The cost of this operation is highly dependent
1479 on the sparsity pattern.
1480
1481 ## iip: In-Place vs Out-Of-Place
1482
1483 For more details on this argument, see the ODEFunction documentation.
1484
1485 ## specialize: Controlling Compilation and Specialization
1486
1487 For more details on this argument, see the ODEFunction documentation.
1488
1489 ## Fields
1490
1491 The fields of the DAEFunction type directly match the names of the inputs.
1492
1493 ## Examples
1494
1495
1496 ### Declaring Explicit Jacobians for DAEs
1497
1498 For fully implicit ODEs (`DAEProblem`s), a slightly different Jacobian function
1499 is necessary. For the DAE
1500
1501 ```math
1502 G(du,u,p,t) = res
1503 ```
1504
1505 The Jacobian should be given in the form `gamma*dG/d(du) + dG/du ` where `gamma`
1506 is given by the solver. This means that the signature is:
1507
1508 ```julia
1509 f(J,du,u,p,gamma,t)
1510 ```
1511
1512 For example, for the equation
1513
1514 ```julia
1515 function testjac(res,du,u,p,t)
1516 res[1] = du[1] - 2.0 * u[1] + 1.2 * u[1]*u[2]
1517 res[2] = du[2] -3 * u[2] - u[1]*u[2]
1518 end
1519 ```
1520
1521 we would define the Jacobian as:
1522
1523 ```julia
1524 function testjac(J,du,u,p,gamma,t)
1525 J[1,1] = gamma - 2.0 + 1.2 * u[2]
1526 J[1,2] = 1.2 * u[1]
1527 J[2,1] = - 1 * u[2]
1528 J[2,2] = gamma - 3 - u[1]
1529 nothing
1530 end
1531 ```
1532
1533 ## Symbolically Generating the Functions
1534
1535 See the `modelingtoolkitize` function from
1536 [ModelingToolkit.jl](https://docs.sciml.ai/ModelingToolkit/stable/) for
1537 automatically symbolically generating the Jacobian and more from the
1538 numerically-defined functions.
1539 """
1540 struct DAEFunction{iip, specialize, F, Ta, Tt, TJ, JVP, VJP, JP, SP, TW, TWt, TPJ, O, TCV,
1541 SYS, ID} <:
1542 AbstractDAEFunction{iip}
1543 f::F
1544 analytic::Ta
1545 tgrad::Tt
1546 jac::TJ
1547 jvp::JVP
1548 vjp::VJP
1549 jac_prototype::JP
1550 sparsity::SP
1551 Wfact::TW
1552 Wfact_t::TWt
1553 paramjac::TPJ
1554 observed::O
1555 colorvec::TCV
1556 sys::SYS
1557 initialization_data::ID
1558 end
1559
1560 """
1561 $(TYPEDEF)
1562 """
1563 abstract type AbstractSDDEFunction{iip} <: AbstractDiffEqFunction{iip} end
1564
1565 @doc doc"""
1566 $(TYPEDEF)
1567
1568 A representation of a SDDE function `f`, defined by:
1569
1570 ```math
1571 M du = f(u,h,p,t) dt + g(u,h,p,t) dW_t
1572 ```
1573
1574 and all of its related functions, such as the Jacobian of `f`, its gradient
1575 with respect to time, and more. For all cases, `u0` is the initial condition,
1576 `p` are the parameters, and `t` is the independent variable.
1577
1578 ## Constructor
1579
1580 ```julia
1581 SDDEFunction{iip,specialize}(f,g;
1582 mass_matrix = __has_mass_matrix(f) ? f.mass_matrix : I,
1583 analytic = __has_analytic(f) ? f.analytic : nothing,
1584 tgrad= __has_tgrad(f) ? f.tgrad : nothing,
1585 jac = __has_jac(f) ? f.jac : nothing,
1586 jvp = __has_jvp(f) ? f.jvp : nothing,
1587 vjp = __has_vjp(f) ? f.vjp : nothing,
1588 jac_prototype = __has_jac_prototype(f) ? f.jac_prototype : nothing,
1589 sparsity = __has_sparsity(f) ? f.sparsity : jac_prototype,
1590 paramjac = __has_paramjac(f) ? f.paramjac : nothing,
1591 colorvec = __has_colorvec(f) ? f.colorvec : nothing
1592 sys = __has_sys(f) ? f.sys : nothing)
1593 ```
1594
1595 Note that only the function `f` itself is required. This function should
1596 be given as `f!(du,u,h,p,t)` or `du = f(u,h,p,t)`. See the section on `iip`
1597 for more details on in-place vs out-of-place handling. The history function
1598 `h` acts as an interpolator over time, i.e. `h(t)` with options matching
1599 the solution interface, i.e. `h(t; save_idxs = 2)`.
1600
1601 All of the remaining functions are optional for improving or accelerating
1602 the usage of `f`. These include:
1603
1604 - `mass_matrix`: the mass matrix `M` represented in the ODE function. Can be used
1605 to determine that the equation is actually a differential-algebraic equation (DAE)
1606 if `M` is singular. Note that in this case special solvers are required, see the
1607 DAE solver page for more details: https://docs.sciml.ai/DiffEqDocs/stable/solvers/dae_solve/.
1608 Must be an AbstractArray or an AbstractSciMLOperator.
1609 - `analytic(u0,p,t)`: used to pass an analytical solution function for the analytical
1610 solution of the ODE. Generally only used for testing and development of the solvers.
1611 - `tgrad(dT,u,h,p,t)` or dT=tgrad(u,p,t): returns ``\frac{\partial f(u,p,t)}{\partial t}``
1612 - `jac(J,u,h,p,t)` or `J=jac(u,p,t)`: returns ``\frac{df}{du}``
1613 - `jvp(Jv,v,h,u,p,t)` or `Jv=jvp(v,u,p,t)`: returns the directional derivative ``\frac{df}{du} v``
1614 - `vjp(Jv,v,h,u,p,t)` or `Jv=vjp(v,u,p,t)`: returns the adjoint derivative ``\frac{df}{du}^\ast v``
1615 - `jac_prototype`: a prototype matrix matching the type that matches the Jacobian. For example,
1616 if the Jacobian is tridiagonal, then an appropriately sized `Tridiagonal` matrix can be used
1617 as the prototype and integrators will specialize on this structure where possible. Non-structured
1618 sparsity patterns should use a `SparseMatrixCSC` with a correct sparsity pattern for the Jacobian.
1619 The default is `nothing`, which means a dense Jacobian.
1620 - `paramjac(pJ,h,u,p,t)`: returns the parameter Jacobian ``\frac{df}{dp}``.
1621 - `colorvec`: a color vector according to the SparseDiffTools.jl definition for the sparsity
1622 pattern of the `jac_prototype`. This specializes the Jacobian construction when using
1623 finite differences and automatic differentiation to be computed in an accelerated manner
1624 based on the sparsity pattern. Defaults to `nothing`, which means a color vector will be
1625 internally computed on demand when required. The cost of this operation is highly dependent
1626 on the sparsity pattern.
1627
1628 ## iip: In-Place vs Out-Of-Place
1629
1630 For more details on this argument, see the ODEFunction documentation.
1631
1632 ## specialize: Controlling Compilation and Specialization
1633
1634 For more details on this argument, see the ODEFunction documentation.
1635
1636 ## Fields
1637
1638 The fields of the DDEFunction type directly match the names of the inputs.
1639 """
1640 struct SDDEFunction{iip, specialize, F, G, TMM, Ta, Tt, TJ, JVP, VJP, JP, SP, TW, TWt, TPJ,
1641 GG, O,
1642 TCV, SYS, ID} <: AbstractSDDEFunction{iip}
1643 f::F
1644 g::G
1645 mass_matrix::TMM
1646 analytic::Ta
1647 tgrad::Tt
1648 jac::TJ
1649 jvp::JVP
1650 vjp::VJP
1651 jac_prototype::JP
1652 sparsity::SP
1653 Wfact::TW
1654 Wfact_t::TWt
1655 paramjac::TPJ
1656 ggprime::GG
1657 observed::O
1658 colorvec::TCV
1659 sys::SYS
1660 initialization_data::ID
1661 end
1662
1663 """

1665 """
1666 abstract type AbstractNonlinearFunction{iip} <: AbstractSciMLFunction{iip} end
1667
1668 @doc doc"""
1669 $(TYPEDEF)
1670
1671 A representation of a nonlinear system of equations `f`, defined by:
1672
1673 ```math
1674 0 = f(u,p)
1675 ```
1676
1677 and all of its related functions, such as the Jacobian of `f`, its gradient
1678 with respect to time, and more. For all cases, `u0` is the initial condition,
1679 `p` are the parameters, and `t` is the independent variable.
1680
1681 ## Constructor
1682
1683 ```julia
1684 NonlinearFunction{iip, specialize}(f;
1685 analytic = __has_analytic(f) ? f.analytic : nothing,
1686 jac = __has_jac(f) ? f.jac : nothing,
1687 jvp = __has_jvp(f) ? f.jvp : nothing,
1688 vjp = __has_vjp(f) ? f.vjp : nothing,
1689 jac_prototype = __has_jac_prototype(f) ? f.jac_prototype : nothing,
1690 sparsity = __has_sparsity(f) ? f.sparsity : jac_prototype,
1691 paramjac = __has_paramjac(f) ? f.paramjac : nothing,
1692 colorvec = __has_colorvec(f) ? f.colorvec : nothing,
1693 sys = __has_sys(f) ? f.sys : nothing)
1694 ```
1695
1696 Note that only the function `f` itself is required. This function should
1697 be given as `f!(du,u,p)` or `du = f(u,p)`. See the section on `iip`
1698 for more details on in-place vs out-of-place handling.
1699
1700 All of the remaining functions are optional for improving or accelerating
1701 the usage of `f`. These include:
1702
1703 - `analytic(u0,p)`: used to pass an analytical solution function for the analytical
1704 solution of the ODE. Generally only used for testing and development of the solvers.
1705 - `jac(J,u,p)` or `J=jac(u,p)`: returns ``\frac{df}{du}``
1706 - `jvp(Jv,v,u,p)` or `Jv=jvp(v,u,p)`: returns the directional derivative ``\frac{df}{du} v``
1707 - `vjp(Jv,v,u,p)` or `Jv=vjp(v,u,p)`: returns the adjoint derivative ``\frac{df}{du}^\ast v``
1708 - `jac_prototype`: a prototype matrix matching the type that matches the Jacobian. For example,
1709 if the Jacobian is tridiagonal, then an appropriately sized `Tridiagonal` matrix can be used
1710 as the prototype and integrators will specialize on this structure where possible. Non-structured
1711 sparsity patterns should use a `SparseMatrixCSC` with a correct sparsity pattern for the Jacobian.
1712 The default is `nothing`, which means a dense Jacobian.
1713 - `paramjac(pJ,u,p)`: returns the parameter Jacobian ``\frac{df}{dp}``.
1714 - `colorvec`: a color vector according to the SparseDiffTools.jl definition for the sparsity
1715 pattern of the `jac_prototype`. This specializes the Jacobian construction when using
1716 finite differences and automatic differentiation to be computed in an accelerated manner
1717 based on the sparsity pattern. Defaults to `nothing`, which means a color vector will be
1718 internally computed on demand when required. The cost of this operation is highly dependent
1719 on the sparsity pattern.
1720
1721 ## iip: In-Place vs Out-Of-Place
1722
1723 For more details on this argument, see the ODEFunction documentation.
1724
1725 ## specialize: Controlling Compilation and Specialization
1726
1727 For more details on this argument, see the ODEFunction documentation.
1728
1729 ## Fields
1730
1731 The fields of the NonlinearFunction type directly match the names of the inputs.
1732 """
1733 struct NonlinearFunction{iip, specialize, F, TMM, Ta, Tt, TJ, JVP, VJP, JP, SP, TW, TWt,
1734 TPJ, O, TCV, SYS, RP, ID} <: AbstractNonlinearFunction{iip}
1735 f::F
1736 mass_matrix::TMM
1737 analytic::Ta
1738 tgrad::Tt
1739 jac::TJ
1740 jvp::JVP
1741 vjp::VJP
1742 jac_prototype::JP
1743 sparsity::SP
1744 Wfact::TW
1745 Wfact_t::TWt
1746 paramjac::TPJ
1747 observed::O
1748 colorvec::TCV
1749 sys::SYS
1750 resid_prototype::RP
1751 initialization_data::ID
1752 end

1754 """
1755 $(TYPEDEF)
1756
1757 A representation of a polynomial nonlinear system of equations given by
1758
1759 ```math
1760 0 = f(polynomialize(u, p), p)
1761 ```
1762
1763 Designed to be used for solving with HomotopyContinuation.
1764
1765 ## Constructor
1766
1767 $(TYPEDSIGNATURES)
1768
1769 Note that only the function `f` is required. This function should be given as `f!(du,u,p)`
1770 or `du = f(u,p)`. See the section on `iip` for more details on in-place vs out-of-place
1771 handling.
1772
1773 To provide the Jacobian function etc, `f` must be a [`NonlinearFunction`](@ref) with the
1774 required fields populated.
1775
1776 ## iip: In-Place vs Out-Of-Place
1777
1778 For more details on this argument, see the ODEFunction documentation.
1779
1780 ## specialize: Controlling Compilation and Specialization
1781
1782 For more details on this argument, see the ODEFunction documentation.
1783
1784 ## Fields
1785
1786 The fields of the `HomotopyNonlinearFunction` type directly match the names of the inputs.
1787
1788 $(FIELDS)
1789 """
1790 struct HomotopyNonlinearFunction{iip, specialize, F, P, Q, D} <:
1791 SciMLBase.AbstractNonlinearFunction{iip}
1792 """
1793 The polynomial function `f`. Stored as a `NonlinearFunction{iip, specialize}`. If not
1794 provided to the constructor as a `NonlinearFunction`, it will be appropriately wrapped.
1795 """
1796 f::F
1797 """
1798 The nonlinear system may be a polynomial of non-polynomial functions. For example,
1799 ```math
1800 sin^2(x^2) + 2sin(x^2) + 1 = 0
1801 log(x + y) ^ 3 = 0.5
1802 ```
1803
1804 is a polynomial in `[sin(x^2), log(x + y)]`. To allow for such systems, `polynomialize`
1805 converts the state vector of the original system (termed as an "original space" vector)
1806 to the state vector of the polynomial system (termed as a "polynomial space" vector).
1807 In the above example, it will be the function:
1808
1809 ```julia
1810 function polynomialize(u, p)
1811 x, y = u
1812 return [sin(x^2), log(x + y)]
1813 end
1814 ```
1815
1816 We refer to `[x, y]` as being in "original space" and `[sin(x^2), log(x + y)]` as being
1817 in "polynomial space".
1818
1819 This defaults to a function which returns `u` as-is.
1820 """
1821 polynomialize::P
1822 """
1823 The inverse operation of `polynomialize`.
1824
1825 This function takes as input a vector `u′` in "polynomial space" and returns a collection of
1826 vectors `uᵢ ∀ i ∈ {1..n}` in "original space" such that `polynomialize(uᵢ, p) == u′ ∀ i`.
1827 A collection is returned since the mapping may not be bijective. For periodic functions
1828 which have infinite such vectors `uᵢ`, it is up to the user to choose which ones to return.
1829
1830 In the aforementioned example in `polynomialize`, this function will be:
1831
1832 ```julia
1833 function unpolynomialize(u, p)
1834 a, b = u
1835 return [
1836 [sqrt(asin(a)), exp(b) - sqrt(asin(a))],
1837 [-sqrt(asin(a)), exp(b) + sqrt(asin(a))],
1838 ]
1839 end
1840 ```
1841
1842 There are of course an infinite number of such functions due to the presence of `sin`.
1843 This example chooses to return the roots in the interval `[-π/2, π/2]`.
1844 """
1845 unpolynomialize::Q
1846 """
1847 A function of the form `denominator(u, p) -> denoms` where `denoms` is an array of
1848 denominator terms which cannot be zero. This is useful when `f` represents the
1849 numerator of a rational function. Roots of `f` which cause any of the values in
1850 `denoms` to be below a threshold will be excluded. Note that here `u` must be in
1851 "polynomial space".
1852 """
1853 denominator::D
1854 end
1855
1856 """
1857 $(TYPEDEF)
1858 """
1859 abstract type AbstractIntervalNonlinearFunction{iip} <: AbstractSciMLFunction{iip} end
1860
1861 @doc doc"""
1862 $(TYPEDEF)

1864 A representation of an interval nonlinear system of equations `f`, defined by:

1873 ## Constructor

1879 ```

1883 for more details on in-place vs out-of-place handling.
1884
1885 All of the remaining functions are optional for improving or accelerating
1886 the usage of `f`. These include:
1887
1888 - `analytic(p)`: used to pass an analytical solution function for the analytical
1889 solution of the ODE. Generally only used for testing and development of the solvers.
1890
1891 ## iip: In-Place vs Out-Of-Place

1902 """
1903 struct IntervalNonlinearFunction{iip, specialize, F, Ta,

1913 """
1914 $(TYPEDEF)
1915
1916 A representation of an objective function `f`, defined by:
1917
1918 ```math
1919 \\min_{u} f(u,p)
1920 ```
1921
1922 and all of its related functions, such as the gradient of `f`, its Hessian,
1923 and more. For all cases, `u` is the state which in this case are the optimization variables and `p` are the fixed parameters or data.
1924
1925 ## Constructor
1926
1927 ```julia
1928 OptimizationFunction{iip}(f, adtype::AbstractADType = NoAD();
1929 grad = nothing, hess = nothing, hv = nothing,
1930 cons = nothing, cons_j = nothing, cons_jvp = nothing,
1931 cons_vjp = nothing, cons_h = nothing,
1932 hess_prototype = nothing,
1933 cons_jac_prototype = nothing,
1934 cons_hess_prototype = nothing,
1935 observed = __has_observed(f) ? f.observed : DEFAULT_OBSERVED_NO_TIME,
1936 lag_h = nothing,
1937 hess_colorvec = __has_colorvec(f) ? f.colorvec : nothing,
1938 cons_jac_colorvec = __has_colorvec(f) ? f.colorvec : nothing,
1939 cons_hess_colorvec = __has_colorvec(f) ? f.colorvec : nothing,
1940 lag_hess_colorvec = nothing,
1941 sys = __has_sys(f) ? f.sys : nothing)
1942 ```
1943
1944 ## Positional Arguments
1945
1946 - `f(u,p)`: the function to optimize. `u` are the optimization variables and `p` are fixed parameters or data used in the objective,
1947 even if no such parameters are used in the objective it should be an argument in the function. For minibatching `p` can be used to pass in
1948 a minibatch, take a look at the tutorial [here](https://docs.sciml.ai/Optimization/stable/tutorials/minibatch/) to see how to do it.
1949 This should return a scalar, the loss value, as the return output.
1950 - `adtype`: see the Defining Optimization Functions via AD section below.
1951
1952 ## Keyword Arguments
1953
1954 - `grad(G,u,p)` or `G=grad(u,p)`: the gradient of `f` with respect to `u`.
1955 - `hess(H,u,p)` or `H=hess(u,p)`: the Hessian of `f` with respect to `u`.
1956 - `hv(Hv,u,v,p)` or `Hv=hv(u,v,p)`: the Hessian-vector product ``(d^2 f / du^2) v``.
1957 - `cons(res,u,p)` or `res=cons(u,p)` : the constraints function, should mutate the passed `res` array
1958 with value of the `i`th constraint, evaluated at the current values of variables
1959 inside the optimization routine. This takes just the function evaluations
1960 and the equality or inequality assertion is applied by the solver based on the constraint
1961 bounds passed as `lcons` and `ucons` to [`OptimizationProblem`](@ref), in case of equality
1962 constraints `lcons` and `ucons` should be passed equal values.
1963 - `cons_j(J,u,p)` or `J=cons_j(u,p)`: the Jacobian of the constraints.
1964 - `cons_jvp(Jv,u,v,p)` or `Jv=cons_jvp(u,v,p)`: the Jacobian-vector product of the constraints.
1965 - `cons_vjp(Jv,u,v,p)` or `Jv=cons_vjp(u,v,p)`: the Jacobian-vector product of the constraints.
1966 - `cons_h(H,u,p)` or `H=cons_h(u,p)`: the Hessian of the constraints, provided as
1967 an array of Hessians with `res[i]` being the Hessian with respect to the `i`th output on `cons`.
1968 - `hess_prototype`: a prototype matrix matching the type that matches the Hessian. For example,
1969 if the Hessian is tridiagonal, then an appropriately sized `Hessian` matrix can be used
1970 as the prototype and optimization solvers will specialize on this structure where possible. Non-structured
1971 sparsity patterns should use a `SparseMatrixCSC` with a correct sparsity pattern for the Hessian.
1972 The default is `nothing`, which means a dense Hessian.
1973 - `cons_jac_prototype`: a prototype matrix matching the type that matches the constraint Jacobian.
1974 The default is `nothing`, which means a dense constraint Jacobian.
1975 - `cons_hess_prototype`: a prototype matrix matching the type that matches the constraint Hessian.
1976 This is defined as an array of matrices, where `hess[i]` is the Hessian w.r.t. the `i`th output.
1977 For example, if the Hessian is sparse, then `hess` is a `Vector{SparseMatrixCSC}`.
1978 The default is `nothing`, which means a dense constraint Hessian.
1979 - `lag_h(res,u,sigma,mu,p)` or `res=lag_h(u,sigma,mu,p)`: the Hessian of the Lagrangian,
1980 where `sigma` is a multiplier of the cost function and `mu` are the Lagrange multipliers
1981 multiplying the constraints. This can be provided instead of `hess` and `cons_h`
1982 to solvers that directly use the Hessian of the Lagrangian.
1983 - `hess_colorvec`: a color vector according to the SparseDiffTools.jl definition for the sparsity
1984 pattern of the `hess_prototype`. This specializes the Hessian construction when using
1985 finite differences and automatic differentiation to be computed in an accelerated manner
1986 based on the sparsity pattern. Defaults to `nothing`, which means a color vector will be
1987 internally computed on demand when required. The cost of this operation is highly dependent
1988 on the sparsity pattern.
1989 - `cons_jac_colorvec`: a color vector according to the SparseDiffTools.jl definition for the sparsity
1990 pattern of the `cons_jac_prototype`.
1991 - `cons_hess_colorvec`: an array of color vector according to the SparseDiffTools.jl definition for
1992 the sparsity pattern of the `cons_hess_prototype`.
1993
1994 When [Symbolic Problem Building with ModelingToolkit](https://docs.sciml.ai/Optimization/stable/tutorials/symbolic/) interface is used the following arguments are also relevant:
1995
1996 - `observed`: an algebraic combination of optimization variables that is of interest to the user
1997 which will be available in the solution. This can be single or multiple expressions.
1998 - `sys`: field that stores the `OptimizationSystem`.
1999
2000 ## Defining Optimization Functions via AD
2001
2002 While using the keyword arguments gives the user control over defining
2003 all of the possible functions, the simplest way to handle the generation
2004 of an `OptimizationFunction` is by specifying an option from ADTypes.jl
2005 which lets the user choose the Automatic Differentiation backend to use
2006 for automatically filling in all of the extra functions. For example,
2007
2008 ```julia
2009 OptimizationFunction(f, AutoForwardDiff())
2010 ```
2011
2012 will use [ForwardDiff.jl](https://github.com/JuliaDiff/ForwardDiff.jl) to define
2013 all of the necessary functions. Note that if any functions are defined
2014 directly, the auto-AD definition does not overwrite the user's choice.
2015
2016 Each of the AD-based constructors are documented separately via their
2017 own dispatches below in the [Automatic Differentiation Construction Choice Recommendations](@ref ad) section.
2018
2019 ## iip: In-Place vs Out-Of-Place
2020
2021 For more details on this argument, see the ODEFunction documentation.
2022
2023 ## specialize: Controlling Compilation and Specialization
2024
2025 For more details on this argument, see the ODEFunction documentation.
2026
2027 ## Fields
2028
2029 The fields of the OptimizationFunction type directly match the names of the inputs.
2030 """
2031 struct OptimizationFunction{
2032 iip, AD, F, G, FG, H, FGH, HV, C, CJ, CJV, CVJ, CH, HP, CJP, CHP, O,
2033 EX, CEX, SYS, LH, LHP, HCV, CJCV, CHCV, LHCV, ID} <:
2034 AbstractOptimizationFunction{iip}
2035 f::F
2036 adtype::AD
2037 grad::G
2038 fg::FG
2039 hess::H
2040 fgh::FGH
2041 hv::HV
2042 cons::C
2043 cons_j::CJ
2044 cons_jvp::CJV
2045 cons_vjp::CVJ
2046 cons_h::CH
2047 hess_prototype::HP
2048 cons_jac_prototype::CJP
2049 cons_hess_prototype::CHP
2050 observed::O
2051 expr::EX
2052 cons_expr::CEX
2053 sys::SYS
2054 lag_h::LH
2055 lag_hess_prototype::LHP
2056 hess_colorvec::HCV
2057 cons_jac_colorvec::CJCV
2058 cons_hess_colorvec::CHCV
2059 lag_hess_colorvec::LHCV
2060 initialization_data::ID
2061 end
2062
2063 """
2064 $(TYPEDEF)
2065 """
2066
2067 struct MultiObjectiveOptimizationFunction{
2068 iip, AD, F, J, H, HV, C, CJ, CJV, CVJ, CH, HP, CJP, CHP, O,
2069 EX, CEX, SYS, LH, LHP, HCV, CJCV, CHCV, LHCV, ID} <:
2070 AbstractOptimizationFunction{iip}
2071 f::F
2072 adtype::AD
2073 jac::J
2074 hess::H
2075 hv::HV
2076 cons::C
2077 cons_j::CJ
2078 cons_jvp::CJV
2079 cons_vjp::CVJ
2080 cons_h::CH
2081 hess_prototype::HP
2082 cons_jac_prototype::CJP
2083 cons_hess_prototype::CHP
2084 observed::O
2085 expr::EX
2086 cons_expr::CEX
2087 sys::SYS
2088 lag_h::LH
2089 lag_hess_prototype::LHP
2090 hess_colorvec::HCV
2091 cons_jac_colorvec::CJCV
2092 cons_hess_colorvec::CHCV
2093 lag_hess_colorvec::LHCV
2094 initialization_data::ID
2095 end
2096
2097 """
2098 $(TYPEDEF)
2099 """
2100 abstract type AbstractODEInputFunction{iip} <: AbstractDiffEqFunction{iip} end
2101
2102 @doc doc"""
2103 $(TYPEDEF)
2104
2105 A representation of a ODE function `f` with inputs, defined by:
2106
2107 ```math
2108 \frac{dx}{dt} = f(x, u, p, t)
2109 ```
2110 where `x` are the states of the system and `u` are the inputs (which may represent
2111 different things in different contexts, such as control variables in optimal control).
2112
2113 Includes all of its related functions, such as the Jacobian of `f`, its gradient
2114 with respect to time, and more. For all cases, `u0` is the initial condition,
2115 `p` are the parameters, and `t` is the independent variable.
2116
2117 ```julia
2118 ODEInputFunction{iip, specialize}(f;
2119 mass_matrix = __has_mass_matrix(f) ? f.mass_matrix : I,
2120 analytic = __has_analytic(f) ? f.analytic : nothing,
2121 tgrad= __has_tgrad(f) ? f.tgrad : nothing,
2122 jac = __has_jac(f) ? f.jac : nothing,
2123 control_jac = __has_controljac(f) ? f.controljac : nothing,
2124 jvp = __has_jvp(f) ? f.jvp : nothing,
2125 vjp = __has_vjp(f) ? f.vjp : nothing,
2126 jac_prototype = __has_jac_prototype(f) ? f.jac_prototype : nothing,
2127 controljac_prototype = __has_controljac_prototype(f) ? f.controljac_prototype : nothing,
2128 sparsity = __has_sparsity(f) ? f.sparsity : jac_prototype,
2129 paramjac = __has_paramjac(f) ? f.paramjac : nothing,
2130 syms = nothing,
2131 indepsym = nothing,
2132 paramsyms = nothing,
2133 colorvec = __has_colorvec(f) ? f.colorvec : nothing,
2134 sys = __has_sys(f) ? f.sys : nothing)
2135 ```
2136
2137 `f` should be given as `f(x_out,x,u,p,t)` or `out = f(x,u,p,t)`.
2138 See the section on `iip` for more details on in-place vs out-of-place handling.
2139
2140 - `mass_matrix`: the mass matrix `M` represented in the BVP function. Can be used
2141 to determine that the equation is actually a BVP for differential algebraic equation (DAE)
2142 if `M` is singular.
2143 - `jac(J,dx,x,u,p,gamma,t)` or `J=jac(dx,x,u,p,gamma,t)`: returns ``\frac{df}{dx}``
2144 - `control_jac(J,du,x,u,p,gamma,t)` or `J=control_jac(du,x,u,p,gamma,t)`: returns ``\frac{df}{du}``
2145 - `jvp(Jv,v,du,x,u,p,gamma,t)` or `Jv=jvp(v,du,x,u,p,gamma,t)`: returns the directional
2146 derivative ``\frac{df}{du} v``
2147 - `vjp(Jv,v,du,x,u,p,gamma,t)` or `Jv=vjp(v,du,x,u,p,gamma,t)`: returns the adjoint
2148 derivative ``\frac{df}{du}^\ast v``
2149 - `jac_prototype`: a prototype matrix matching the type that matches the Jacobian. For example,
2150 if the Jacobian is tridiagonal, then an appropriately sized `Tridiagonal` matrix can be used
2151 as the prototype and integrators will specialize on this structure where possible. Non-structured
2152 sparsity patterns should use a `SparseMatrixCSC` with a correct sparsity pattern for the Jacobian.
2153 The default is `nothing`, which means a dense Jacobian.
2154 - `controljac_prototype`: a prototype matrix matching the type that matches the Jacobian. For example,
2155 if the Jacobian is tridiagonal, then an appropriately sized `Tridiagonal` matrix can be used
2156 as the prototype and integrators will specialize on this structure where possible. Non-structured
2157 sparsity patterns should use a `SparseMatrixCSC` with a correct sparsity pattern for the Jacobian.
2158 The default is `nothing`, which means a dense Jacobian.
2159 - `paramjac(pJ,x,u,p,t)`: returns the parameter Jacobian ``\frac{df}{dp}``.
2160 - `colorvec`: a color vector according to the SparseDiffTools.jl definition for the sparsity
2161 pattern of the `jac_prototype`. This specializes the Jacobian construction when using
2162 finite differences and automatic differentiation to be computed in an accelerated manner
2163 based on the sparsity pattern. Defaults to `nothing`, which means a color vector will be
2164 internally computed on demand when required. The cost of this operation is highly dependent
2165 on the sparsity pattern.
2166

2168 For more details on this argument, see the ODEFunction documentation.

2171 For more details on this argument, see the ODEFunction documentation.
